newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans stuck in rebel-held Goma pray for peace.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans stuck in rebel-held Goma pray for peace.

text.p: Christmas prayers for peace held a special poignancy for civilians in rebel-held eastern Zaire, where they fear a successful counter-offensive by the Zairean army.
The Roman Catholic cathedral in Goma, the largest city taken by rebels, was packed with hundreds of worshippers for a "midnight" mass, which ended three hours early because of security concerns.

"What can we do but pray? We have nowhere to run to if the army comes back here," said Justin Bijiga, voicing widespread fears that a successful Zairean army counter-offensive might be imminent following the return of President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Nervous Goma residents streamed quickly into the night towards their homes from the incense-filled hall of the cathedral, made from black lava stone.

But rebel leader Laurent Kabila told Reuters on Wednesday a Zairean counter-offensive had been beaten back and his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire had seized the town of Bunia, 360 km (220 miles) north of Goma.
The rebels have previously exaggerated claims to have taken several towns including Bunia, but Kabila said his report was correct this time. No independent confirmation was available.

"People are scared because they have been under Mobutu for so long. But for many this is the first peaceful Christmas they have known in their lifetimes," said Kabila, an opponent of Mobutu since the 1960s.

This former lakeside resort was sleepier than usual on Wednesday in contrast to Christmas a year ago when fighting erupted between drunken factions of the ill-disciplined Zairean army killing up to 100, according to aid workers.
Mobutu's return to Zaire last week after four months in Europe convalescing after cancer surgery prompted hundreds of people to flee Goma, doubtful of the rebels' power to defend them.
The rebels have seized a swath of Zaire's eastern territory about 500 km (300 miles) long running from north to south since October, but doubts have arisen as to the durability of the alliance.
"Reports of confrontations between the rebels and Mai-Mai have not made anyone feel any easier," said one aid worker.
Kabila said his troops had begun disarming the Mai-Mai and would train them following reports they attacked local people.
The Mai-Mai are a highly volatile band of Zairean fighters including children who believe bullets turn to water if their chiefs innoculate them with a secret vaccine.
Their reputation for fearlessness spearheaded the rebel advance through North Kivu province, sending Zairean troops on an orgy of looting before they fled long in advance of the Mai-Mai arriving.
The Mai-Mai army include children as young as 10 years old and their main motives for fighting seemed to be looting and the desire for territorial control.
The Mai-Mai take their name from the Swahili word for water and their arms include crossbows, spears and home-made shotguns.
The departure of some expatriate aid workers from Goma for the Christmas holiday alarmed residents, who fear the Zairean army will be more ruthless on its return.
"May be they (foreign aid workers) know something we don't and they have been warned about an attack," said Bosco Katembo.
The civil war in eastern Zaire began in October when the government tried to expel the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group which migrated to Zaire from Rwanda up to 200 years ago.
The Banyamulenge, backed by Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army, took up arms and allied themselves with other opposition groups.
